title: Why mourners say it
hookLine: after a parent dies, many say Kaddish for eleven months and each year after, with a minyan answering

cards: It's a Tuesday morning, seven a.m., in a small synagogue. Nine people are waiting, checking the door. A woman whose father died last month needs ten to say Kaddish.
Someone makes a phone call. A neighbor comes in, still in running clothes, and sits down. Now there are ten.
She stands and says the words, and as she pauses, the room answers her, out loud. This happens in towns all over the world, every morning and evening, for months on end.
Why does a mourner need a room full of people to say one prayer?

teach.b: Start with the rule. Kaddish is a prayer of holiness, and Jewish law says those are said only with a minyan, a quorum of ten. So a mourner can't say it alone.
That's not a technicality: the mourner has to come out of the house, and the community has to show up. How did the Kaddish become the mourner's prayer at all?
A medieval story is told about Rabbi Akiva. He meets a dead man's soul carrying wood, in torment.

Akiva finds the man's young son, teaches him to stand in the congregation and lead the praise, and the father's soul is released. The story spread through medieval Europe, and the custom spread with it. How long?

Many say Kaddish for eleven months after a parent dies. Tradition held that a soul's judgment could last up to twelve months, and children stop at eleven so as not to suggest their parent needed the full year.

Then, every year on the anniversary of the death, the yahrzeit, they say it again. Who says it? In many communities, sons and daughters both; in Orthodox communities, customs for daughters differ from place to place.
And what does it do for the mourner? At the hardest moment of their life, a mourner stands and says: may God's name be magnified. They don't have to feel it.
They just have to say it, and the room answers.

how: Mourners say the Mourner's Kaddish at daily services with a minyan, traditionally for eleven months after a parent's death and on each yahrzeit; many congregations make sure a minyan gathers so mourners can say it, and the congregation answers aloud.

games.q: you're a mourner at a weekday service. there are only nine people. what happens?
o: wait or call around until there are ten.
skip it for the rest of the year.
games.why: the Kaddish needs ten. communities call around, and a neighbor walking in can make the minyan.

practice: Bring to mind someone who says Kaddish, a friend who lost a parent this year, someone in your family years ago, maybe you, and picture them standing to praise while they grieve.
Then picture yourself in that room as one of the ten, and hold them there for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Kaddish. A prayer of holiness, said by a mourner only with ten people there to answer it.
